name: Beverly Hills diet

card.summary: A 1981 celebrity-era weight-loss plan from Judy Mazel built on fruit phases and food combining, aimed at a leaner body and slimmer face.
card.aka: Beverly Hills Diet, New Beverly Hills Diet
card.note: A 1981 JAMA report warned that heavy fruit intake with little salt could cause dangerous fluid and electrolyte loss.

quick.overview:
The Beverly Hills Diet is a weight-loss plan created by Judy Mazel and published in 1981. It begins with days of eating only specific fruits in a set order, then adds other foods in stages, and it never combines carbohydrates and proteins at the same meal. The goal people attach to it is fast fat loss and a leaner body.

The book spent 30 weeks on the New York Times bestseller list and sold over a million copies. Nutrition experts classify it as a fad diet built on food combining, and a 1981 medical journal report raised safety concerns about its fruit-heavy early phases.
quick.how: The original plan runs in stages: about ten days of specific fruits eaten in order, then bread, butter and corn introduced from around day 11, with complete proteins only from about day 19. Foods are sorted into groups and kept apart. An updated 1996 edition shortened the program to 35 days and added a longer-term phase.
quick.risks: A 1981 JAMA report found no scientific support for the program's theory and warned that large fruit intake with little salt could cause fluid loss, fever, weakness, rapid pulse and dangerously low blood pressure. A nutritionist quoted in coverage listed diarrhea, low potassium and irregular heartbeat. Dietitians note that weight lost comes from severe calorie restriction.

lead: The Beverly Hills Diet was created by author Judy Mazel (1943 to 2007) and published in 1981 by Macmillan [1]. Mazel developed it after about six months with a nutritionist in Santa Fe, New Mexico, having lost roughly 70 pounds, and then opened a weight-loss clinic in Los Angeles with celebrity clients [1].

The plan claims digestive enzymes act differently on different foods, so what matters is when and with what a food is eaten [1]. The first 10 days allow only particular fruits in a prescribed order, days 11 to 18 add bread, butter and corn, and complete proteins such as steak or lobster start on day 19 [1]. Carbohydrates and proteins are never eaten together or on the same day [1].

The book was a New York Times bestseller for 30 weeks and sold over a million copies [1]. Mazel published The New Beverly Hills Diet in 1996, shortening the plan to 35 days and adding a long-term phase with similar food-combining rules [1]. Nutrition experts classify the diet as a fad based on food combining [1].

chain: Weight loss and a leaner body and face
angle.text: People used the plan to lose weight quickly, which changes body shape and facial fullness. Dietitians note that the loss comes from severe calorie and nutrient restriction.

paras: Mazel's book arrived in 1981 amid the Los Angeles celebrity diet boom, and her clinic in the city served high-profile clients [1]. The plan's staged structure and its fruit-only opening made it widely discussed [1].

The diet's theory is that enzymes in different foods interact so that undigested food turns to fat, and that correctly ordered, separated foods let the body burn it off [1]. Foods are divided into carbohydrate, protein and fat groups, with carbohydrates split into fruit and three tiers [1].

A 1981 JAMA report by Gabe Mirkin and Ronald Shore found no scientific support for the program and said it contradicted established medical nutrition knowledge [1]. They questioned the claim that undigested food causes weight gain [1]. Nutritionist Theodore Labuza has called it unbalanced [1]. Dietitians observe that any weight loss reflects severe calorie and nutrient restriction and that the strict rules are hard to sustain [1].

The JAMA authors warned that heavy fruit intake with little salt could cause dangerous fluid loss, leading to fever, weakness, rapid pulse and a drop in blood pressure severe enough to be fatal [1]. Labuza listed diarrhea, low potassium and irregular heartbeat as risks [1].
No studies found. The main published evaluation is a 1981 JAMA report, which was a critique of the program rather than a trial [1].

timeline.event: The Beverly Hills Diet is published by Macmillan and a JAMA report critiques it [1].
The New Beverly Hills Diet published with a 35-day plan [1].
